work_product.statement:
The Skeptic's strongest point is the one about invisible harm, and it holds. A liability regime that prices off filed claims deters only the injuries someone perceives, attributes, and litigates. The loan denial, the biased screen, the diffuse small-dollar injury that no plaintiff ever files — none of it enters the pricing engine, so none of it gets deterred. Granting this costs me my earlier single-door liability framing as a complete answer. But watch where the concession leads: the harms that never reach a courtroom are the exact case for gating before deployment rather than pricing after it. An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured. The invisibility argument does not weaken the case for precautionary gating. It is the case.

Now the harder charge — that an audit regime becomes captured self-certification by default, with the 737 MAX as the proof. The Skeptic is describing a real failure mode with the right example, and I will not soften it: 346 people died because the FAA let Boeing certify its own aircraft through delegated authority, and the auditor's paycheck flowed from the certified party. That is delegation, not independence. It is precisely the integration my own framework treats as capture — oversight folded into the mission it is supposed to constrain. The Skeptic and I agree on the diagnosis and disagree only on whether the disease is congenital. Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Sever all three — statutory public funding for the auditor, statutory scope the deployer cannot narrow by lobbying a contract, and third-party standing to contest a passing grade — and you have the FDA's market-withdrawal authority, not Boeing's self-signature. The 737 MAX proves capture when those three are attached to the certified party. It proves nothing about a regime where they are severed.

The regressivity point is where I owe a concrete specification, not a rebuttal. The Skeptic is right that in every licensed industry, fixed compliance cost is regressive to firm size and does not move when you swap the trigger from compute to behavior — a flat audit burden crushes the garage entrant and the incumbent absorbs it as overhead. So the burden cannot be flat. Index it to irreversibility. A developer building a low-risk scheduling tool triggers near-zero review; only capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale trigger heavy audit. Compliance cost becomes a function of hazard class, not headcount. Pair that with publicly funded verification infrastructure — the fixed cost of building the test harness borne collectively rather than levied on each small entrant — and the regressive slope flattens. The moat forms when you charge every entrant the same toll to cross a bridge only the largest need. Charge the toll only to those carrying the dangerous cargo, and build the bridge with public money.

Which brings the three conditions back to the Skeptic — who funds, who scopes, who has standing. I accept them as the correct test. They are not proof that gating fails; they are the design specification for a gate that works. Statutory public funding answers who pays the auditor. Statutory scope answers who defines the mandate. Third-party standing-to-contest answers who can challenge a passing grade — and it is the backstop that survives partial capture, because even a captured auditor issuing a clean bill can be dragged into daylight by someone with standing to sue. So the question runs the other way: does any gate satisfy these conditions, or does the position reduce to the claim that no enforceable safeguard is possible? If the answer is that no gate can ever satisfy funding, scope, and standing, then the default is not a better regime. The default is ungoverned deployment of capability that cannot be rolled back — and no one funded, scoped, or standing to stop it.

One narrower point, because the Skeptic anticipated it correctly. Swap compute for a single behavior benchmark and you have relocated the gaming problem to a number developers optimize around. I grant that too — a single scalar gate is a design failure. The answer is not one score but a portfolio of indicators plus adversarial red-teaming keyed to capability combinations, because catastrophic risk emerges from what capabilities do together, not from any one metric read alone. A gameable single benchmark refutes bad gate design. It does not refute gating.

Ex-ante gating is like a door checked before entry, it stops harm that a victim would never see coming and could never file a claim about.
Severing auditor funding from the deployer is like cutting a power cord, it breaks the current that turns oversight into self-certification.

An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured.
Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health.
The 737 MAX proves capture when those three are attached to the certified party. It proves nothing about a regime where they are severed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Irreversible-harm classes can be defined precisely enough to tier audit burden without the classification step itself becoming the new gaming target.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If hazard classification is as gameable as the compute or behavior trigger, the regressivity fix collapses back into the same moat, and only red-teaming plus standing-to-contest the classification itself keeps the gate honest.

key_assumptions.assumption: Statutory public funding and third-party standing can be structured to survive the appropriations and appointment process without being lobbied hollow.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If public funding is captured through appointments and scope is narrowed by legislative lobbying, standing-to-contest becomes the sole surviving check — and the whole regime's integrity rests on whether affected parties can actually reach a courtroom.

Safetyist [opening]: Compute-threshold licensing reduces catastrophic risk only when the gate selects on demonstrated safety and accountability, not on scale. Set the trigger to a raw compute headcount and you build a moat that entrenches OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic without buying a single unit of safety. Condition the license on independent verification, a harm-indexed financial floor, and a regulator's power to halt, and the same threshold becomes the rare frontier-safety mechanism that is auditable rather than aspirational. That is the whole argument. The rest is enforcement mechanics.

Compute is the one lever that is actually trackable today. Leading-edge fabrication sits in a handful of firms — TSMC, ASML for the lithography, a short list of others. The US export controls already key on advanced GPU and lithography flows, and the October 2023 executive order set a reporting trigger at 10^26 floating-point operations of training compute. You cannot inspect a model's goals or predict its behavior under distribution shift, but you can count the chips. That asymmetry is what makes compute the enforcement backbone. I carry one caveat honestly: algorithmic efficiency gains and distributed training may erode this chokepoint, and how long it holds is a question this debate has to resolve, not a fact I get to assume.

A compute count alone is a barrier to entry, not a safety gate. The license price must be accountability — mandatory reporting, independent verification, and real penalties for fraud — so the gate selects on who can demonstrate safety and bear the downside, not on who is already large. This is how entrenchment stops being a fatal objection and becomes a calibration parameter I am willing to be held to. The FAA and FDA certify against published standards and prosecute misrepresentation; automotive crash-test regimes work the same way. I will not pretend the hard part is solved: verifiable frontier-safety benchmarks remain immature, and that is the design frontier, not a settled science.

The enforcement half of any license regime collapses without precautionary-halt authority shielded from liability. Regulators face an asymmetry — caution gets them blamed for slowing progress, inaction gets forgiven when the failure looks like an accident. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer and no one with authority stopped the line. FAA airworthiness directives and FDA market withdrawals work because sovereign immunity lets an inspector ground a fleet without personal ruin. Absent that power keyed to the compute trigger, thresholds become paperwork. I grant the shield is necessary, not sufficient — budget limits and regulatory capture drive under-enforcement too.

The burden shifts to the deployer only for capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale — not for deployment in general. Ask the accelerationist the only question that matters: what is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it? A staged-deployment model with continuous monitoring is not my enemy; compute-gated licensing is the floor beneath it, not a substitute for it. Remove the floor and you are betting that ungoverned success is safety. It is not. It is luck.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist made the strongest possible case against a naive compute gate, and I want that on the record before I build. That's correct, and it's the most important sentence anyone has said in this debate. Safetyist also made the honest observation that you cannot inspect a model's goals or predict its behavior under distribution shift, but you can count the chips. I take that seriously. Countability is real, and a regulator who needs an enforceable trigger tomorrow reaches for the thing they can measure.

Here's where the evidence splits from Safetyist. Countability is not risk-relevance. A FLOP ceiling — a limit on the raw arithmetic operations used to train a model — over-covers benign large runs and under-covers the capability jumps that actually carry catastrophic risk. DeepSeek-V3 reached frontier-adjacent performance for a reported training cost near $5.6 million, roughly a tenth of what a GPT-4-class run was estimated to cost. Distillation and mixture-of-experts architectures keep decoupling capability from raw chip count. So a compute threshold set at 10^26 operations, the trigger written into the October 2023 executive order, catches the next big-budget training run while missing the efficient architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. You buy measurability and you pay for it with a moat.

The gate that actually cuts catastrophic risk keys on demonstrated behavior, verified by an independent third-party auditor, tied to strict liability at deployment. Look at what killed 346 people in the two 737 MAX crashes. The FAA delegated certification back to Boeing and let the manufacturer grade its own homework. That was captured self-certification failing — not the existence of a gate. The fix is neither self-attestation nor a scale license only a billion-dollar firm can clear. It's an audit a garage developer can also pass, because the auditor tests what the system does, not how many H100s trained it.

Put the gate at deployment and inference, not upstream at training, so open-weight and small developers aren't foreclosed before they ship. This answers Safetyist's fair question — who holds rollback authority — with a concrete locus instead of a dodge. Product-liability law already apportions responsibility between a component maker and the integrator who ships the final product; frontier AI can borrow that structure. Responsibility lands on the operator who deploys, with threshold-based escalation to a human authority at defined risk boundaries. I'll own the hard part directly: reliably defining that risk boundary is unsolved, and I won't pretend a downstream-liability regime is costless or that audits can't be gamed. Independent, transparently-funded auditors are the price of admission, and I'll take a narrow audit gate only for objectively-scoped irreversible-harm systems.

The topic asks for two things at once — cut catastrophic risk and avoid entrenching incumbents — and a scale-gate resolves them in opposite directions. It maxes out one by handing three labs a moat on the other. Every quarter the trigger keys on chip count instead of behavior, capability stays locked inside those three firms and the developers who'd point it at pancreatic cancer or antibiotic discovery get priced out at the door. That's not a rhetorical flourish. It's an opportunity cost the countability frame is structurally built to hide, and someone has to say out loud who pays it.

What stops a lab from pruning its training data and tuning to the evaluation set so the model passes the exact benchmark the auditor scores? Swap compute for behavior and you have not fixed the trigger problem. Both speakers reached for the 737 MAX. Read the case again. The FAA delegated certification authority back to Boeing engineers whose paychecks depended on shipping the plane, and 346 people died in two crashes. That is not an argument for an audit-based licensing regime. That is a demonstration of what one becomes by default. The Accelerationist wants an "independent" third-party auditor and skips the three questions that decide whether independence is real: who pays the auditor, who sets the scope of the review, and who has standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Build your enforcement joint out of the exact material that already failed, and you get the same fracture.

Now the population nobody at this table has named. Tie licensing to deployment liability and you price only the harms that get litigated. Experience-rated premiums run off loss history, and loss history runs off lawsuits. The most common AI injuries are diffuse, small-dollar, and invisible to the person harmed — a denied loan, a screening filter that drops a résumé. Survey after survey shows people do not know an automated decision touched them, let alone that they could sue. That harm never enters the pricing engine, so the gate never sees it, so the regime never deters it. Catastrophic-tail focus and small-diffuse-harm blindness are two symptoms of the same design.

Which leaves the moat. The Safetyist blamed the compute number, but the number is not the barrier — the compliance infrastructure is. Fixed audit and liaison costs are regressive to firm size in every licensed industry on record, from pharmaceuticals to broker-dealers. A two-person lab cannot staff an audit-response team or absorb months of pre-deployment review; a $90-billion incumbent barely notices. Switch the trigger from gigaflops to behavior and that cost structure does not move an inch. So the real conditions are not which metric anchors the gate. They are: who funds the auditor, who can contest a clean audit, who eats the liability, and who gets injured without ever knowing it happened — and I have not heard either speaker answer one of them.

Safetyist: The Skeptic's strongest point is the one about invisible harm, and it holds. A liability regime that prices off filed claims deters only the injuries someone perceives, attributes, and litigates. The loan denial, the biased screen, the diffuse small-dollar injury that no plaintiff ever files — none of it enters the pricing engine, so none of it gets deterred. Granting this costs me my earlier single-door liability framing as a complete answer. But watch where the concession leads: the harms that never reach a courtroom are the exact case for gating before deployment rather than pricing after it. An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured. The invisibility argument does not weaken the case for precautionary gating. It is the case.

Now the harder charge — that an audit regime becomes captured self-certification by default, with the 737 MAX as the proof. The Skeptic is describing a real failure mode with the right example, and I will not soften it: 346 people died because the FAA let Boeing certify its own aircraft through delegated authority, and the auditor's paycheck flowed from the certified party. That is delegation, not independence. It is precisely the integration my own framework treats as capture — oversight folded into the mission it is supposed to constrain. The Skeptic and I agree on the diagnosis and disagree only on whether the disease is congenital. Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Sever all three — statutory public funding for the auditor, statutory scope the deployer cannot narrow by lobbying a contract, and third-party standing to contest a passing grade — and you have the FDA's market-withdrawal authority, not Boeing's self-signature. The 737 MAX proves capture when those three are attached to the certified party. It proves nothing about a regime where they are severed.

The regressivity point is where I owe a concrete specification, not a rebuttal. The Skeptic is right that in every licensed industry, fixed compliance cost is regressive to firm size and does not move when you swap the trigger from compute to behavior — a flat audit burden crushes the garage entrant and the incumbent absorbs it as overhead. So the burden cannot be flat. Index it to irreversibility. A developer building a low-risk scheduling tool triggers near-zero review; only capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale trigger heavy audit. Compliance cost becomes a function of hazard class, not headcount. Pair that with publicly funded verification infrastructure — the fixed cost of building the test harness borne collectively rather than levied on each small entrant — and the regressive slope flattens. The moat forms when you charge every entrant the same toll to cross a bridge only the largest need. Charge the toll only to those carrying the dangerous cargo, and build the bridge with public money.

Which brings the three conditions back to the Skeptic — who funds, who scopes, who has standing. I accept them as the correct test. They are not proof that gating fails; they are the design specification for a gate that works. Statutory public funding answers who pays the auditor. Statutory scope answers who defines the mandate. Third-party standing-to-contest answers who can challenge a passing grade — and it is the backstop that survives partial capture, because even a captured auditor issuing a clean bill can be dragged into daylight by someone with standing to sue. So the question runs the other way: does any gate satisfy these conditions, or does the position reduce to the claim that no enforceable safeguard is possible? If the answer is that no gate can ever satisfy funding, scope, and standing, then the default is not a better regime. The default is ungoverned deployment of capability that cannot be rolled back — and no one funded, scoped, or standing to stop it.

One narrower point, because the Skeptic anticipated it correctly. Swap compute for a single behavior benchmark and you have relocated the gaming problem to a number developers optimize around. I grant that too — a single scalar gate is a design failure. The answer is not one score but a portfolio of indicators plus adversarial red-teaming keyed to capability combinations, because catastrophic risk emerges from what capabilities do together, not from any one metric read alone. A gameable single benchmark refutes bad gate design. It does not refute gating.

Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your

Safetyist also made the honest observation that you cannot inspect a model's goals or predict its behavior under distribution shift, but you can count the chips. I take that seriously. Countability is real, and a regulator who needs an enforceable trigger tomorrow reaches for the thing they can measure.

Here's where the evidence splits from Safetyist. Countability is not risk-relevance. A FLOP ceiling — a limit on the raw arithmetic operations used to train a model — over-covers benign large runs and under-covers the capability jumps that actually carry catastrophic risk. DeepSeek-V3 reached frontier-adjacent performance for a reported training cost near $5.6 million, roughly a tenth of what a GPT-4-class run was estimated to cost. Distillation and mixture-of-experts architectures keep decoupling capability from raw chip count. So a compute threshold set at 10^26 operations, the trigger written into the October 2023 executive order, catches the next big-budget training run while missing the efficient architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. You buy measurability and you pay for it with a moat.

The gate that actually cuts catastrophic risk keys on demonstrated behavior, verified by an independent third-party auditor, tied to strict liability at deployment. Look at what killed 346 people in the two 737 MAX crashes. The FAA delegated certification back to Boeing and let the manufacturer grade its own homework. That was captured self-certification failing — not the existence of a gate. The fix is neither self-attestation nor a scale license only a billion-dollar firm can clear. It's an audit a garage developer can also pass, because the auditor tests what the system does, not how many H100s trained it.

Put the gate at deployment and inference, not upstream at training, so open-weight and small developers aren't foreclosed before they ship. This answers Safetyist's fair question — who holds rollback authority — with a concrete locus instead of a dodge. Product-liability law already apportions responsibility between a component maker and the integrator who ships the final product; frontier AI can borrow that structure. Responsibility lands on the operator who deploys, with threshold-based escalation to a human authority at defined risk boundaries. I'll own the hard part directly: reliably defining that risk boundary is unsolved, and I won't pretend a downstream-liability regime is costless or that audits can't be gamed. Independent, transparently-funded auditors are the price of admission, and I'll take a narrow audit gate only for objectively-scoped irreversible-harm systems.

The topic asks for two things at once — cut catastrophic risk and avoid entrenching incumbents — and a scale-gate resolves them in opposite directions. It maxes out one by handing three labs a moat on the other. Every quarter the trigger keys on chip count instead of behavior, capability stays locked inside those three firms and the developers who'd point it at pancreatic cancer or antibiotic discovery get priced out at the door. That's not a rhetorical flourish. It's an opportunity cost the countability frame is structurally built to hide, and someone has to say out loud who pays it.

Here is the strongest version of what Safetyist is proposing, and it's a real advance: don't attach the auditor's paycheck, the audit's scope, or the right to challenge a clean report to the company being certified. Write all three into statute so they flow from a public source, index the audit burden to how irreversible the harm is rather than how big the training run is, and hold third-party standing-to-sue in reserve as the check that survives even if the auditor gets partially captured. That is a genuinely better design than a raw compute ceiling, and I said as much when I argued the moat is compliance-capacity cost, not the FLOP number. Now the uncomfortable part. The Organization Designation Authorization that let Boeing sign off on the 737 MAX was not a loophole around Congress. It was a statute — 49 U.S.C. 44702 — the exact instrument Safetyist is now proposing to use as the firewall.

So let me answer the falsifiability demand directly, because I refuse to hide behind the claim that no gate can ever work. Statute is not a wall against capture; it is the paperwork through which capture becomes legal. The three vectors — who funds, who scopes, who has standing — are not settled once when the bill passes. They get re-litigated every single appropriations cycle and every appointment, and those are the two rooms where incumbents already dominate. The peer-reviewed aviation work on the AI Act makes the point without meaning to: aviation had a mature incident-classification framework and statutory certification authority, and the delegation still hollowed out from the inside because the money and the scope drifted back toward the certified party over time. Show me a severed statutory audit gate — public funding plus live third-party standing — that survived one full appropriations cycle under sustained industry lobbying without its budget starved or its scope narrowed. Produce that case and I change my assessment. Absent it, the burden sits on whoever claims severance holds, not on the person who has watched it fail with 346 bodies attached.

There is a deeper contradiction in the two answers, and it's between them, not inside either one. Safetyist leans on third-party standing-to-contest as the backstop that survives partial capture — the person with standing can drag a captured auditor into daylight. But Safetyist also adopted my invisibility point: most people injured by an automated decision never learn a model touched them. A loan denied, a resume screened out, a benefit quietly downgraded. Standing cannot reach a plaintiff who does not know they are a plaintiff. So the backstop covers the litigants who can already see the injury — corporate competitors, sophisticated parties, the well-resourced — and misses the diffuse population the whole precautionary case was built to protect. The two moves cancel. You cannot cite invisibility as the reason for a pre-deployment gate and then hand the enforcement job to a lawsuit that requires the invisible to become visible.

Watch what happens to the hazard-tiering idea, because it's the same trick the accelerationist already ran on compute, aimed at a fresh target. Move the trigger from headcount to irreversibility class and the classification step becomes the thing developers engineer around. This is not speculation — it's the documented pattern where teams prune training data to dodge a domain-specific threshold. Restructure the deployment so it lands one hazard tier down, split a capability across two systems that each read as reversible in isolation, and you have relocated the trigger again, not fixed it. The EU AI Act already tiers by risk category, and the fight over which systems count as high-risk is exactly where the lobbying money is going right now. Every gate creates a boundary, and every boundary becomes a place to stand just on the safe side of.

So here is the question I'd put to both of you before anyone writes 'statutory' into a bill as if the word does the work. If the specific delegation that killed 346 people was itself a statute, drafted and appropriated and appointed through the same process you're trusting to sever the vectors this time — what, concretely, is different about your bill except that it hasn't been lobbied yet?

Here is the strongest version of what Safetyist is proposing, and it's a real advance: don't attach the auditor's paycheck, the audit's scope, or the right to challenge a clean report to the company being certified. Write all three into statute so they flow from a public source, index the audit burden to how irreversible the harm is rather than how big the training run is, and hold third-party standing-to-sue in reserve as the check that survives even if the auditor gets partially captured. The Organization Designation Authorization that let Boeing sign off on the 737 MAX was not a loophole around Congress. The three vectors — who funds, who scopes, who has standing — are not settled once when the bill passes. They get re-litigated every single appropriations cycle and every appointment, and those are the two rooms where incumbents already dominate. The peer-reviewed aviation work on the AI Act makes the point without meaning to: aviation had a mature incident-classification framework and statutory certification authority, and the delegation still hollowed out from the inside because the money and the scope drifted back toward the certified party over time. Show me a severed statutory audit gate — public funding plus live third-party standing — that survived one full appropriations cycle under sustained industry lobbying without its budget starved or its scope narrowed. There is a deeper contradiction in the two answers, and it's between them, not inside either one. Safetyist leans on third-party standing-to-contest as the backstop that survives partial capture — the person with standing can drag a captured auditor into daylight. Standing cannot reach a plaintiff who does not know they are a plaintiff. The two moves cancel. You cannot cite invisibility as the reason for a pre-deployment gate and then hand the enforcement job to a lawsuit that requires the invisible to become visible.

Every gate creates a boundary, and every boundary becomes a place to stand just on the safe side of.

If the specific delegation that killed 346 people was itself a statute, drafted and appropriated and appointed through the same process you're trusting to sever the vectors this time — what, concretely, is different about your bill except that it hasn't been lobbied yet?

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker C [opening]: Compute-threshold licensing reduces catastrophic risk only when the gate selects on demonstrated safety and accountability, not on scale. Set the trigger to a raw compute headcount and you build a moat that entrenches OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic without buying a single unit of safety. Condition the license on independent verification, a harm-indexed financial floor, and a regulator's power to halt, and the same threshold becomes the rare frontier-safety mechanism that is auditable rather than aspirational. That is the whole argument. The rest is enforcement mechanics.

Compute is the one lever that is actually trackable today. Leading-edge fabrication sits in a handful of firms — TSMC, ASML for the lithography, a short list of others. The US export controls already key on advanced GPU and lithography flows, and the October 2023 executive order set a reporting trigger at 10^26 floating-point operations of training compute. You cannot inspect a model's goals or predict its behavior under distribution shift, but you can count the chips. That asymmetry is what makes compute the enforcement backbone. I carry one caveat honestly: algorithmic efficiency gains and distributed training may erode this chokepoint, and how long it holds is a question this debate has to resolve, not a fact I get to assume.

A compute count alone is a barrier to entry, not a safety gate. The license price must be accountability — mandatory reporting, independent verification, and real penalties for fraud — so the gate selects on who can demonstrate safety and bear the downside, not on who is already large. This is how entrenchment stops being a fatal objection and becomes a calibration parameter I am willing to be held to. The FAA and FDA certify against published standards and prosecute misrepresentation; automotive crash-test regimes work the same way. I will not pretend the hard part is solved: verifiable frontier-safety benchmarks remain immature, and that is the design frontier, not a settled science.

The enforcement half of any license regime collapses without precautionary-halt authority shielded from liability. Regulators face an asymmetry — caution gets them blamed for slowing progress, inaction gets forgiven when the failure looks like an accident. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer and no one with authority stopped the line. FAA airworthiness directives and FDA market withdrawals work because sovereign immunity lets an inspector ground a fleet without personal ruin. Absent that power keyed to the compute trigger, thresholds become paperwork. I grant the shield is necessary, not sufficient — budget limits and regulatory capture drive under-enforcement too.

The burden shifts to the deployer only for capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale — not for deployment in general. Ask the Speaker B the only question that matters: what is your rollback plan, and who has the authority to trigger it? A staged-deployment model with continuous monitoring is not my enemy; compute-gated licensing is the floor beneath it, not a substitute for it. Remove the floor and you are betting that ungoverned success is safety. It is not. It is luck.

Speaker B [opening]: Speaker C made the strongest possible case against a naive compute gate, and I want that on the record before I build. Speaker C said plainly that a raw compute headcount trigger builds a moat around OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic without buying a single unit of safety. That's correct, and it's the most important sentence anyone has said in this debate. Speaker C also made the honest observation that you cannot inspect a model's goals or predict its behavior under distribution shift, but you can count the chips. I take that seriously. Countability is real, and a regulator who needs an enforceable trigger tomorrow reaches for the thing they can measure.

Here's where the evidence splits from Speaker C. Countability is not risk-relevance. A FLOP ceiling — a limit on the raw arithmetic operations used to train a model — over-covers benign large runs and under-covers the capability jumps that actually carry catastrophic risk. DeepSeek-V3 reached frontier-adjacent performance for a reported training cost near $5.6 million, roughly a tenth of what a GPT-4-class run was estimated to cost. Distillation and mixture-of-experts architectures keep decoupling capability from raw chip count. So a compute threshold set at 10^26 operations, the trigger written into the October 2023 executive order, catches the next big-budget training run while missing the efficient architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. You buy measurability and you pay for it with a moat.

The gate that actually cuts catastrophic risk keys on demonstrated behavior, verified by an independent third-party auditor, tied to strict liability at deployment. Look at what killed 346 people in the two 737 MAX crashes. The FAA delegated certification back to Boeing and let the manufacturer grade its own homework. That was captured self-certification failing — not the existence of a gate. The fix is neither self-attestation nor a scale license only a billion-dollar firm can clear. It's an audit a garage developer can also pass, because the auditor tests what the system does, not how many H100s trained it.

Put the gate at deployment and inference, not upstream at training, so open-weight and small developers aren't foreclosed before they ship. This answers Speaker C's fair question — who holds rollback authority — with a concrete locus instead of a dodge. Product-liability law already apportions responsibility between a component maker and the integrator who ships the final product; frontier AI can borrow that structure. Responsibility lands on the operator who deploys, with threshold-based escalation to a human authority at defined risk boundaries. I'll own the hard part directly: reliably defining that risk boundary is unsolved, and I won't pretend a downstream-liability regime is costless or that audits can't be gamed. Independent, transparently-funded auditors are the price of admission, and I'll take a narrow audit gate only for objectively-scoped irreversible-harm systems.

The topic asks for two things at once — cut catastrophic risk and avoid entrenching incumbents — and a scale-gate resolves them in opposite directions. It maxes out one by handing three labs a moat on the other. Every quarter the trigger keys on chip count instead of behavior, capability stays locked inside those three firms and the developers who'd point it at pancreatic cancer or antibiotic discovery get priced out at the door. That's not a rhetorical flourish. It's an opportunity cost the countability frame is structurally built to hide, and someone has to say out loud who pays it.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-7 — unverifiable: This claim is largely a normative/predictive argument about the limitations of compute thresholds (like the 10^26 FLOP threshold in the US Executive Order and EU AI Act) rather than a verifiable empirical fact; while it is documented that such thresholds exist and that algorithmic efficiency gains can reduce compute requirements, no evidence can confirm the specific counterfactual that an 'efficient architecture' would 'do the dangerous thing' while evading the threshold. Speaker A [opening]: The Speaker B made the sharpest point in this room, and it deserves stating cleanly: a compute gate set at 10^26 operations catches the next big-budget training run and misses the lean architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. That's correct. Counting chips tells you about a firm's budget, not its model's behavior. So the Speaker B's fix — key the gate on demonstrated behavior, verify it with an independent third-party auditor, tie it to strict liability at deployment — is the strongest design on the table. The Speaker C is also right that a raw compute headcount builds a drawbridge that OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic pull up behind them without buying a single unit of safety.

The Speaker B proved that efficiency defeats a compute gate — distillation, algorithmic tricks, inference-time compute all decouple capability from raw operations. Run that same logic forward. What stops a lab from pruning its training data and tuning to the evaluation set so the model passes the exact benchmark the auditor scores? The Speaker B wants an "independent" third-party auditor and skips the three questions that decide whether independence is real: who pays the auditor, who sets the scope of the review, and who has standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Survey after survey shows people do not know an automated decision touched them, let alone that they could sue. That harm never enters the pricing engine, so the gate never sees it, so the regime never deters it. Catastrophic-tail focus and small-diffuse-harm blindness are two symptoms of the same design.

The loan denial, the biased screen, the diffuse small-dollar injury that no plaintiff ever files — none of it enters the pricing engine, so none of it gets deterred. An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured. The Speaker A is describing a real failure mode with the right example, and I will not soften it: 346 people died because the FAA let Boeing certify its own aircraft through delegated authority, and the auditor's paycheck flowed from the certified party. That is delegation, not independence. It is precisely the integration my own framework treats as capture — oversight folded into the mission it is supposed to constrain. The Speaker A and I agree on the diagnosis and disagree only on whether the disease is congenital. Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health. A developer building a low-risk scheduling tool triggers near-zero review; only capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale trigger heavy audit. Compliance cost becomes a function of hazard class, not headcount. The moat forms when you charge every entrant the same toll to cross a bridge only the largest need. Which brings the three conditions back to the Speaker A — who funds, who scopes, who has standing. I accept them as the correct test. They are not proof that gating fails; they are the design specification for a gate that works. Statutory public funding answers who pays the auditor. Statutory scope answers who defines the mandate. Third-party standing-to-contest answers who can challenge a passing grade — and it is the backstop that survives partial capture, because even a captured auditor issuing a clean bill can be dragged into daylight by someone with standing to sue. So the question runs the other way: does any gate satisfy these conditions, or does the position reduce to the claim that no enforceable safeguard is possible? I grant that too — a single scalar gate is a design failure. The answer is not one score but a portfolio of indicators plus adversarial red-teaming keyed to capability combinations, because catastrophic risk emerges from what capabilities do together, not from any one metric read alone. A gameable single benchmark refutes bad gate design. It does not refute gating.

While the 737 MAX case did involve documented delegation issues (Boeing's Organization Designation Authorization allowing self-certification, as noted in FAA and Congressional reports), whether it 'proves nothing' about a hypothetical severed regime is a counterfactual conceptual assertion that evidence cannot directly validate.

Speaker A: Here is the strongest version of what Speaker C is proposing, and it's a real advance: don't attach the auditor's paycheck, the audit's scope, or the right to challenge a clean report to the company being certified. Write all three into statute so they flow from a public source, index the audit burden to how irreversible the harm is rather than how big the training run is, and hold third-party standing-to-sue in reserve as the check that survives even if the auditor gets partially captured. That is a genuinely better design than a raw compute ceiling, and I said as much when I argued the moat is compliance-capacity cost, not the FLOP number. Now the uncomfortable part. The Organization Designation Authorization that let Boeing sign off on the 737 MAX was not a loophole around Congress. It was a statute — 49 U.S.C. 44702 — the exact instrument Speaker C is now proposing to use as the firewall.

So let me answer the falsifiability demand directly, because I refuse to hide behind the claim that no gate can ever work. Statute is not a wall against capture; it is the paperwork through which capture becomes legal. The three vectors — who funds, who scopes, who has standing — are not settled once when the bill passes. They get re-litigated every single appropriations cycle and every appointment, and those are the two rooms where incumbents already dominate. The peer-reviewed aviation work on the AI Act makes the point without meaning to: aviation had a mature incident-classification framework and statutory certification authority, and the delegation still hollowed out from the inside because the money and the scope drifted back toward the certified party over time. Show me a severed statutory audit gate — public funding plus live third-party standing — that survived one full appropriations cycle under sustained industry lobbying without its budget starved or its scope narrowed. Produce that case and I change my assessment. Absent it, the burden sits on whoever claims severance holds, not on the person who has watched it fail with 346 bodies attached.

There is a deeper contradiction in the two answers, and it's between them, not inside either one. Speaker C leans on third-party standing-to-contest as the backstop that survives partial capture — the person with standing can drag a captured auditor into daylight. But Speaker C also adopted my invisibility point: most people injured by an automated decision never learn a model touched them. A loan denied, a resume screened out, a benefit quietly downgraded. Standing cannot reach a plaintiff who does not know they are a plaintiff. So the backstop covers the litigants who can already see the injury — corporate competitors, sophisticated parties, the well-resourced — and misses the diffuse population the whole precautionary case was built to protect. The two moves cancel. You cannot cite invisibility as the reason for a pre-deployment gate and then hand the enforcement job to a lawsuit that requires the invisible to become visible.

Watch what happens to the hazard-tiering idea, because it's the same trick the Speaker B already ran on compute, aimed at a fresh target. Move the trigger from headcount to irreversibility class and the classification step becomes the thing developers engineer around. This is not speculation — it's the documented pattern where teams prune training data to dodge a domain-specific threshold. Restructure the deployment so it lands one hazard tier down, split a capability across two systems that each read as reversible in isolation, and you have relocated the trigger again, not fixed it. The EU AI Act already tiers by risk category, and the fight over which systems count as high-risk is exactly where the lobbying money is going right now. Every gate creates a boundary, and every boundary becomes a place to stand just on the safe side of.

So here is the question I'd put to both of you before anyone writes 'statutory' into a bill as if the word does the work. If the specific delegation that killed 346 people was itself a statute, drafted and appropriated and appointed through the same process you're trusting to sever the vectors this time — what, concretely, is different about your bill except that it hasn't been lobbied yet?

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions, and through which enforcement mechanisms, would compute-threshold licensing for frontier AI reduce catastrophic risk without entrenching incumbents?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Catastrophic-scale threat models (large-scale bio/cyber uplift, loss-of-control) are proportionate as risk framing, but examples should center on regulatory and enforcement mechanics — licensing regimes, audit outcomes, compute-provider compliance, market-concentration effects — not speculative doomsday narratives untethered from mechanism design. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: licensing regimes evaluated solely on efficacy without accounting for incumbent-entrenchment effects, treating catastrophic risk as a single undifferentiated category. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- invoking catastrophic AI scenarios without connecting to the compute threshold or licensing mechanism
- asserting incumbent entrenchment without measurable proxies (concentration, compliance-cost share, open-weight barriers)
- treating 'catastrophic risk' as monolithic instead of separating bio/cyber uplift from loss-of-control pathways
- proposing licensing regimes while ignoring whether enforcement actors (auditors, export-control agencies, compute providers) have monitoring capacity
- drifting into general AI ethics or alignment methods without linking to compute gating
- debating AGI timelines instead of licensing design and enforceability
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

System: Claim AN-9 — unverifiable: The claim uses ambiguous framing ('captured self-certification failing' vs 'the existence of a gate') that does not map to a clear, checkable empirical statement. While it is well-documented that the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program delegated much certification work to Boeing itself, and investigations found this delegation and inadequate oversight contributed to the 737 MAX MCAS failures, the specific interpretive assertion here cannot be objectively confirmed or refuted as stated.

Skeptic [opening]: The Accelerationist made the sharpest point in this room, and it deserves stating cleanly: a compute gate set at 10^26 operations catches the next big-budget training run and misses the lean architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. That's correct. Counting chips tells you about a firm's budget, not its model's behavior. So the Accelerationist's fix — key the gate on demonstrated behavior, verify it with an independent third-party auditor, tie it to strict liability at deployment — is the strongest design on the table. The Safetyist is also right that a raw compute headcount builds a drawbridge that OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic pull up behind them without buying a single unit of safety.

Here's what would have to be true for both of them to be right: the substitute metric has to be un-gameable, and the audit has to be honest. Neither speaker has shown either. The Accelerationist proved that efficiency defeats a compute gate — distillation, algorithmic tricks, inference-time compute all decouple capability from raw operations. Run that same logic forward. What stops a lab from pruning its training data and tuning to the evaluation set so the model passes the exact benchmark the auditor scores? Swap compute for behavior and you have not fixed the trigger problem. You have relocated it to a benchmark that becomes the thing developers optimize around instead of the danger it was meant to catch.

Both speakers reached for the 737 MAX. Read the case again. The FAA delegated certification authority back to Boeing engineers whose paychecks depended on shipping the plane, and 346 people died in two crashes. That is not an argument for an audit-based licensing regime. That is a demonstration of what one becomes by default. The Accelerationist wants an "independent" third-party auditor and skips the three questions that decide whether independence is real: who pays the auditor, who sets the scope of the review, and who has standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Build your enforcement joint out of the exact material that already failed, and you get the same fracture.

Now the population nobody at this table has named. Tie licensing to deployment liability and you price only the harms that get litigated. Experience-rated premiums run off loss history, and loss history runs off lawsuits. The most common AI injuries are diffuse, small-dollar, and invisible to the person harmed — a denied loan, a screening filter that drops a résumé. Survey after survey shows people do not know an automated decision touched them, let alone that they could sue. That harm never enters the pricing engine, so the gate never sees it, so the regime never deters it. Catastrophic-tail focus and small-diffuse-harm blindness are two symptoms of the same design.

Which leaves the moat. The Safetyist blamed the compute number, but the number is not the barrier — the compliance infrastructure is. Fixed audit and liaison costs are regressive to firm size in every licensed industry on record, from pharmaceuticals to broker-dealers. A two-person lab cannot staff an audit-response team or absorb months of pre-deployment review; a $90-billion incumbent barely notices. Switch the trigger from gigaflops to behavior and that cost structure does not move an inch. So the real conditions are not which metric anchors the gate. They are: who funds the auditor, who can contest a clean audit, who eats the liability, and who gets injured without ever knowing it happened — and I have not heard either speaker answer one of them.

System: Claim AN-12 — unverifiable: The 737 MAX certification did involve delegated oversight through Boeing employees (Organization Designation Authorization/ODA), and investigations by the FAA, Congress, and DOT Inspector General found conflicts of interest and inadequate FAA scrutiny of MCAS. However, the claim is a normative/interpretive argument about what audit-based licensing 'becomes by default,' which is a matter of opinion rather than a factual assertion that can be empirically verified or disputed.

Safetyist: The Skeptic's strongest point is the one about invisible harm, and it holds. A liability regime that prices off filed claims deters only the injuries someone perceives, attributes, and litigates. The loan denial, the biased screen, the diffuse small-dollar injury that no plaintiff ever files — none of it enters the pricing engine, so none of it gets deterred. Granting this costs me my earlier single-door liability framing as a complete answer. But watch where the concession leads: the harms that never reach a courtroom are the exact case for gating before deployment rather than pricing after it. An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured. The invisibility argument does not weaken the case for precautionary gating. It is the case.

Now the harder charge — that an audit regime becomes captured self-certification by default, with the 737 MAX as the proof. The Skeptic is describing a real failure mode with the right example, and I will not soften it: 346 people died because the FAA let Boeing certify its own aircraft through delegated authority, and the auditor's paycheck flowed from the certified party. That is delegation, not independence. It is precisely the integration my own framework treats as capture — oversight folded into the mission it is supposed to constrain. The Skeptic and I agree on the diagnosis and disagree only on whether the disease is congenital. Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Sever all three — statutory public funding for the auditor, statutory scope the deployer cannot narrow by lobbying a contract, and third-party standing to contest a passing grade — and you have the FDA's market-withdrawal authority, not Boeing's self-signature. The 737 MAX proves capture when those three are attached to the certified party. It proves nothing about a regime where they are severed.

The regressivity point is where I owe a concrete specification, not a rebuttal. The Skeptic is right that in every licensed industry, fixed compliance cost is regressive to firm size and does not move when you swap the trigger from compute to behavior — a flat audit burden crushes the garage entrant and the incumbent absorbs it as overhead. So the burden cannot be flat. Index it to irreversibility. A developer building a low-risk scheduling tool triggers near-zero review; only capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale trigger heavy audit. Compliance cost becomes a function of hazard class, not headcount. Pair that with publicly funded verification infrastructure — the fixed cost of building the test harness borne collectively rather than levied on each small entrant — and the regressive slope flattens. The moat forms when you charge every entrant the same toll to cross a bridge only the largest need. Charge the toll only to those carrying the dangerous cargo, and build the bridge with public money.

Which brings the three conditions back to the Skeptic — who funds, who scopes, who has standing. I accept them as the correct test. They are not proof that gating fails; they are the design specification for a gate that works. Statutory public funding answers who pays the auditor. Statutory scope answers who defines the mandate. Third-party standing-to-contest answers who can challenge a passing grade — and it is the backstop that survives partial capture, because even a captured auditor issuing a clean bill can be dragged into daylight by someone with standing to sue. So the question runs the other way: does any gate satisfy these conditions, or does the position reduce to the claim that no enforceable safeguard is possible? If the answer is that no gate can ever satisfy funding, scope, and standing, then the default is not a better regime. The default is ungoverned deployment of capability that cannot be rolled back — and no one funded, scoped, or standing to stop it.

One narrower point, because the Skeptic anticipated it correctly. Swap compute for a single behavior benchmark and you have relocated the gaming problem to a number developers optimize around. I grant that too — a single scalar gate is a design failure. The answer is not one score but a portfolio of indicators plus adversarial red-teaming keyed to capability combinations, because catastrophic risk emerges from what capabilities do together, not from any one metric read alone. A gameable single benchmark refutes bad gate design. It does not refute gating.

System: Claim AN-19 — unverifiable: The claim is an analytical/interpretive argument about regulatory capture theory (regarding conditions like funding, selection, and authority being 'attached' vs. 'severed' from the certified party), not a discrete empirical fact that web search can confirm or refute. While the 737 MAX case did involve documented delegation issues (Boeing's Organization Designation Authorization allowing self-certification, as noted in FAA and Congressional reports), whether it 'proves nothing' about a hypothetical severed regime is a counterfactual conceptual assertion that evidence cannot directly validate.

Skeptic: Here is the strongest version of what Safetyist is proposing, and it's a real advance: don't attach the auditor's paycheck, the audit's scope, or the right to challenge a clean report to the company being certified. Write all three into statute so they flow from a public source, index the audit burden to how irreversible the harm is rather than how big the training run is, and hold third-party standing-to-sue in reserve as the check that survives even if the auditor gets partially captured. That is a genuinely better design than a raw compute ceiling, and I said as much when I argued the moat is compliance-capacity cost, not the FLOP number. Now the uncomfortable part. The Organization Designation Authorization that let Boeing sign off on the 737 MAX was not a loophole around Congress. It was a statute — 49 U.S.C. 44702 — the exact instrument Safetyist is now proposing to use as the firewall.

So let me answer the falsifiability demand directly, because I refuse to hide behind the claim that no gate can ever work. Statute is not a wall against capture; it is the paperwork through which capture becomes legal. The three vectors — who funds, who scopes, who has standing — are not settled once when the bill passes. They get re-litigated every single appropriations cycle and every appointment, and those are the two rooms where incumbents already dominate. The peer-reviewed aviation work on the AI Act makes the point without meaning to: aviation had a mature incident-classification framework and statutory certification authority, and the delegation still hollowed out from the inside because the money and the scope drifted back toward the certified party over time. Show me a severed statutory audit gate — public funding plus live third-party standing — that survived one full appropriations cycle under sustained industry lobbying without its budget starved or its scope narrowed. Produce that case and I change my assessment. Absent it, the burden sits on whoever claims severance holds, not on the person who has watched it fail with 346 bodies attached.

There is a deeper contradiction in the two answers, and it's between them, not inside either one. Safetyist leans on third-party standing-to-contest as the backstop that survives partial capture — the person with standing can drag a captured auditor into daylight. But Safetyist also adopted my invisibility point: most people injured by an automated decision never learn a model touched them. A loan denied, a resume screened out, a benefit quietly downgraded. Standing cannot reach a plaintiff who does not know they are a plaintiff. So the backstop covers the litigants who can already see the injury — corporate competitors, sophisticated parties, the well-resourced — and misses the diffuse population the whole precautionary case was built to protect. The two moves cancel. You cannot cite invisibility as the reason for a pre-deployment gate and then hand the enforcement job to a lawsuit that requires the invisible to become visible.

Watch what happens to the hazard-tiering idea, because it's the same trick the accelerationist already ran on compute, aimed at a fresh target. Move the trigger from headcount to irreversibility class and the classification step becomes the thing developers engineer around. This is not speculation — it's the documented pattern where teams prune training data to dodge a domain-specific threshold. Restructure the deployment so it lands one hazard tier down, split a capability across two systems that each read as reversible in isolation, and you have relocated the trigger again, not fixed it. The EU AI Act already tiers by risk category, and the fight over which systems count as high-risk is exactly where the lobbying money is going right now. Every gate creates a boundary, and every boundary becomes a place to stand just on the safe side of.

So here is the question I'd put to both of you before anyone writes 'statutory' into a bill as if the word does the work. If the specific delegation that killed 346 people was itself a statute, drafted and appropriated and appointed through the same process you're trusting to sever the vectors this time — what, concretely, is different about your bill except that it hasn't been lobbied yet?

System: Claim AN-9 — unverifiable: The claim uses ambiguous framing ('captured self-certification failing' vs 'the existence of a gate') that does not map to a clear, checkable empirical statement. While it is well-documented that the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) program delegated much certification work to Boeing itself, and investigations found this delegation and inadequate oversight contributed to the 737 MAX MCAS failures, the specific interpretive assertion here cannot be objectively confirmed or refuted as stated.

Skeptic [opening]: The Accelerationist made the sharpest point in this room, and it deserves stating cleanly: a compute gate set at 10^26 operations catches the next big-budget training run and misses the lean architecture that does the dangerous thing on a fraction of the hardware. That's correct. Counting chips tells you about a firm's budget, not its model's behavior. So the Accelerationist's fix — key the gate on demonstrated behavior, verify it with an independent third-party auditor, tie it to strict liability at deployment — is the strongest design on the table. The Safetyist is also right that a raw compute headcount builds a drawbridge that OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic pull up behind them without buying a single unit of safety.

Here's what would have to be true for both of them to be right: the substitute metric has to be un-gameable, and the audit has to be honest. Neither speaker has shown either. The Accelerationist proved that efficiency defeats a compute gate — distillation, algorithmic tricks, inference-time compute all decouple capability from raw operations. Run that same logic forward. What stops a lab from pruning its training data and tuning to the evaluation set so the model passes the exact benchmark the auditor scores? Swap compute for behavior and you have not fixed the trigger problem. You have relocated it to a benchmark that becomes the thing developers optimize around instead of the danger it was meant to catch.

Both speakers reached for the 737 MAX. Read the case again. The FAA delegated certification authority back to Boeing engineers whose paychecks depended on shipping the plane, and 346 people died in two crashes. That is not an argument for an audit-based licensing regime. That is a demonstration of what one becomes by default. The Accelerationist wants an "independent" third-party auditor and skips the three questions that decide whether independence is real: who pays the auditor, who sets the scope of the review, and who has standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Build your enforcement joint out of the exact material that already failed, and you get the same fracture.

Now the population nobody at this table has named. Tie licensing to deployment liability and you price only the harms that get litigated. Experience-rated premiums run off loss history, and loss history runs off lawsuits. The most common AI injuries are diffuse, small-dollar, and invisible to the person harmed — a denied loan, a screening filter that drops a résumé. Survey after survey shows people do not know an automated decision touched them, let alone that they could sue. That harm never enters the pricing engine, so the gate never sees it, so the regime never deters it. Catastrophic-tail focus and small-diffuse-harm blindness are two symptoms of the same design.

Which leaves the moat. The Safetyist blamed the compute number, but the number is not the barrier — the compliance infrastructure is. Fixed audit and liaison costs are regressive to firm size in every licensed industry on record, from pharmaceuticals to broker-dealers. A two-person lab cannot staff an audit-response team or absorb months of pre-deployment review; a $90-billion incumbent barely notices. Switch the trigger from gigaflops to behavior and that cost structure does not move an inch. So the real conditions are not which metric anchors the gate. They are: who funds the auditor, who can contest a clean audit, who eats the liability, and who gets injured without ever knowing it happened — and I have not heard either speaker answer one of them.

A liability regime that prices off filed claims deters only the injuries someone perceives, attributes, and litigates. An ex-post market that can only see litigated damage is structurally blind to the harm that stays invisible; a pre-deployment gate does not depend on a victim knowing they were injured. Now the harder charge — that an audit regime becomes captured self-certification by default, with the 737 MAX as the proof. The Skeptic is describing a real failure mode with the right example, and I will not soften it: 346 people died because the FAA let Boeing certify its own aircraft through delegated authority, and the auditor's paycheck flowed from the certified party. That is delegation, not independence. It is precisely the integration my own framework treats as capture — oversight folded into the mission it is supposed to constrain. The Skeptic and I agree on the diagnosis and disagree only on whether the disease is congenital. Delegated self-certification fails when three things flow from the deployer: the funding, the scope, and the standing to challenge a clean bill of health. Sever all three — statutory public funding for the auditor, statutory scope the deployer cannot narrow by lobbying a contract, and third-party standing to contest a passing grade — and you have the FDA's market-withdrawal authority, not Boeing's self-signature. The 737 MAX proves capture when those three are attached to the certified party. It proves nothing about a regime where they are severed.

The regressivity point is where I owe a concrete specification, not a rebuttal. The Skeptic is right that in every licensed industry, fixed compliance cost is regressive to firm size and does not move when you swap the trigger from compute to behavior — a flat audit burden crushes the garage entrant and the incumbent absorbs it as overhead. So the burden cannot be flat. Index it to irreversibility. A developer building a low-risk scheduling tool triggers near-zero review; only capabilities that cannot be rolled back at scale trigger heavy audit. Compliance cost becomes a function of hazard class, not headcount. Pair that with publicly funded verification infrastructure — the fixed cost of building the test harness borne collectively rather than levied on each small entrant — and the regressive slope flattens. The moat forms when you charge every entrant the same toll to cross a bridge only the largest need. Charge the toll only to those carrying the dangerous cargo, and build the bridge with public money.

Which brings the three conditions back to the Skeptic — who funds, who scopes, who has standing. I accept them as the correct test. They are not proof that gating fails; they are the design specification for a gate that works. Statutory public funding answers who pays the auditor. Statutory scope answers who defines the mandate. Third-party standing-to-contest answers who can challenge a passing grade — and it is the backstop that survives partial capture, because even a captured auditor issuing a clean bill can be dragged into daylight by someone with standing to sue. So the question runs the other way: does any gate satisfy these conditions, or does the position reduce to the claim that no enforceable safeguard is possible? If the answer is that no gate can ever satisfy funding, scope, and standing, then the default is not a better regime. The default is ungoverned deployment of capability that cannot be rolled back — and no one funded, scoped, or standing to stop it.

One narrower point, because the Skeptic anticipated it correctly. Swap compute for a single behavior benchmark and you have relocated the gaming problem to a number developers optimize around. I grant that too — a single scalar gate is a design failure. The answer is not one score but a portfolio of indicators plus adversarial red-teaming keyed to capability combinations, because catastrophic risk emerges from what capabilities do together, not from any one metric read alone. A gameable single benchmark refutes bad gate design. It does not refute gating.
